NONPROFIT MUTUAL BENEFIT CORPORATION — FORMATION INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Trade Alliance

REQUIRED CONTENT OF NONPROFIT MUTUAL BENEFIT CORPORATION ARTICLES
California's Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law contains its own required-content statute for a mutual benefit corporation's articles of incorporation, separate from the required-content statute that governs a nonprofit public benefit corporation and separate again from the one that governs an ordinary for-profit corporation. The mutual benefit statute requires the filed articles to state: the corporation's name; a specific, statutorily prescribed statement that the corporation "is a nonprofit mutual benefit corporation organized under the Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law" and that its purpose "is to engage in any lawful act or activity, other than credit union business, for which a corporation may be organized under such law" (two narrow exceptions substitute other prescribed purpose language for a corporation formed under the California Credit Union Law or as a statutorily defined public bank, and the articles may, but need not, add a further definition of the corporation's purposes); the name and California street address of the corporation's initial agent for service of process; the corporation's initial street address; and its initial mailing address, if that differs from the street address. Unlike the required content for a nonprofit public benefit corporation's articles, the mutual benefit statute's fixed statement does not ask the incorporator to elect "public" or "charitable" purposes, and does not make any further purpose description mandatory — a further description is optional in every case for a mutual benefit corporation, where it is mandatory for a public benefit corporation electing "public" purposes. As with a nonprofit public benefit corporation, nothing in this list calls for a statement of authorized shares — a nonprofit mutual benefit corporation has no shareholders and issues no stock; it has members instead.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The articles of incorporation of a corporation formed under this part shall set forth the following: (a) The name of the corporation. (b) (1) Except as provided in paragraph (2) or (3), the following statement: “This corporation is a nonprofit mutual benefit corporation organized under the Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law. The purpose of this corporation is to engage in any lawful act or activity, other than credit union business, for which a corporation may be organized under such law.”"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 7130(a)-(b)(1), California Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law, the required name and statutory purpose statement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=7130.)
  "(c) The name and street address in this state of the corporation’s initial agent for service of process in accordance with subdivision (b) of Section 8210. (d) The initial street address of the corporation. (e) The initial mailing address of the corporation, if different from the initial street address."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 7130(c)-(e), California Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law, agent for service of process and required addresses (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=7130.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what one state's required formation-document content for this specific type of nonprofit corporation looks like — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation's formation, and required content for a nonprofit corporation's founding filing varies by state. The two citations below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 7130, so they are treated as one source, not two independent ones. This document is informational only: it does not itself form any corporation, file anything with the California Secretary of State, or determine whether any corporation qualifies for federal tax-exempt status, which is a separate determination made by the Internal Revenue Service under federal law, not by this document or by the California statute it describes.

MUTUAL BENEFIT PURPOSE DISTINGUISHED FROM PUBLIC BENEFIT PURPOSE
California's Nonprofit Corporation Law separates its three nonprofit corporation types by statute, not merely by convention, and a mutual benefit corporation's authorizing statute states the dividing line in its own text. A corporation may be formed under the Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law "for any lawful purpose," but the same statute affirmatively bars from that part any corporation whose assets are irrevocably dedicated to charitable, religious, or public purposes and which, by law or by its own articles or bylaws, must distribute its assets on dissolution to a person carrying on a charitable, religious, or public purpose — that kind of corporation belongs instead under the Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law or the Nonprofit Religious Corporation Law. The mutual benefit naming statute reinforces the same line from the other direction: the Secretary of State will not file mutual benefit articles setting forth a name that "may create the impression that the purpose of the corporation is public, charitable, or religious or that it is a charitable foundation." Read together, these are the statutory basis for describing a mutual benefit corporation's purpose as something other than a public or charitable one — an organization such as a trade association, homeowners association, business league, or social club, formed for a lawful purpose that does not carry the irrevocable public/charitable asset dedication a public benefit or religious corporation carries, and whose formation filing and name may not represent that it does.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Subject to any other provision of law of this state applying to the particular class of corporation or line of activity, a corporation may be formed under this part for any lawful purpose; provided that a corporation all of the assets of which are irrevocably dedicated to charitable, religious, or public purposes and which as a matter of law or according to its articles or bylaws must, upon dissolution, distribute its assets to a person or persons carrying on a charitable, religious, or public purpose or purposes may not be formed under this part."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 7111, California Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law, the "any lawful purpose" authorization and its charitable/religious/public-purpose exclusion (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=7111.)
  "(b) The Secretary of State shall not file articles pursuant to this part setting forth a name that may create the impression that the purpose of the corporation is public, charitable, or religious or that it is a charitable foundation."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 7122(b), California Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law, the bar on names implying a public, charitable, or religious purpose (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=7122.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of how that one state's Corporations Code itself draws the line between a mutual benefit and a public benefit purpose — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation, and the mutual/public benefit distinction, and the vocabulary used to describe it, vary by state. The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code § 7111 and Cal. Corp. Code § 7122, and are treated as two independent sources, not subsections of one section. This document is informational only: it does not itself form any corporation and does not determine which nonprofit category best fits a specific organization's activities or a specific corporation's federal tax-exempt status, which is a separate IRS determination this document does not make.

FEDERAL TAX-EXEMPT STATUS IS A SEPARATE FEDERAL QUESTION THE STATE STATUTE DOES NOT ANSWER
Nothing in California's Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law — including the required purpose statement discussed above — addresses federal tax-exempt status; the state formation statute governs only what must appear in the articles filed with the California Secretary of State, and is silent on the separate question of federal tax treatment. Federal tax-exempt recognition is governed entirely by the Internal Revenue Code and administered by the IRS, under provisions distinct from the 26 U.S.C. § 501(c)(3) charitable-organization status commonly associated with public benefit corporations. Because a mutual benefit corporation's own statutory purpose is not limited to charitable, religious, or public purposes, a mutual benefit corporation is not the kind of organization § 501(c)(3) describes; organizations of the kind California law calls "mutual benefit" — for example trade associations, business leagues, or civic and social welfare organizations — more commonly correspond to other Internal Revenue Code categories, such as § 501(c)(4), covering "civic leagues or organizations not organized for profit but operated exclusively for the promotion of social welfare," or § 501(c)(6), covering "business leagues, chambers of commerce, real-estate boards, boards of trade" and similar organizations not organized for profit. Each of those federal categories has its own separate eligibility requirements under federal law, and qualifying for one is a distinct, later step from forming the corporation under California's mutual benefit statute; the state statute does not require, guarantee, or evaluate eligibility for any of them.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(4)(A) Civic leagues or organizations not organized for profit but operated exclusively for the promotion of social welfare, or local associations of employees, the membership of which is limited to the employees of a designated person or persons in a particular municipality, and the net earnings of which are devoted exclusively to charitable, educational, or recreational purposes."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 501(c)(4)(A), Internal Revenue Code, civic leagues and social welfare organizations exemption category (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title26-section501&num=0&edition=prelim)
  "(6) Business leagues, chambers of commerce, real-estate boards, boards of trade, or professional football leagues (whether or not administering a pension fund for football players), not organized for profit and no part of the net earnings of which inures to the benefit of any private shareholder or individual."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 501(c)(6), Internal Revenue Code, business leagues and similar organizations exemption category (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title26-section501&num=0&edition=prelim)

The two federal citations below are subsections of the same Internal Revenue Code section, 26 U.S.C. § 501(c), so they are treated as one source illustrating a category of federal provisions, not two independent corroborating sources, and they are not exhaustive of every federal exemption category a mutual benefit-type organization might potentially fit. This document is informational only: it does not itself form any corporation and does not determine federal tax-exempt status for any organization under any Internal Revenue Code provision — that determination is made by the IRS, not by this document or by the California statute it describes.

DISTRIBUTIONS TO MEMBERS RESTRICTED OUTSIDE OF DISSOLUTION
California's Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law contains its own distributions chapter, and its central rule reads, on its face, almost the same as the flat no-distributions rule that applies to a nonprofit public benefit corporation: "no corporation shall make any distribution except upon dissolution," subject only to a narrow carve-out letting a corporation purchase or redeem memberships, itself conditioned on meeting further statutory requirements found elsewhere in the same chapter. That provision, by its own terms, does not apply to the winding-up and dissolution process itself — dissolution-stage asset distribution is instead governed by a separate set of statutes. Put together, these two sections mean that while a mutual benefit corporation is an ongoing, operating entity, it is barred from distributing its earnings or assets to its members in the way a business corporation pays dividends to shareholders, aside from the narrow membership purchase-or-redemption exception; the statutory feature that actually distinguishes a mutual benefit corporation from a public benefit corporation is not a general license to pay profits to members while operating, but rather what happens to remaining assets specifically at dissolution, addressed in a separate clause below.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "This chapter does not apply to any proceeding for winding up and dissolution of corporations under Chapters 15 (commencing with Section 8510), 16 (commencing with Section 8610), and 17 (commencing with Section 8710)."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 7410, California Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law, the distributions chapter's inapplicability to dissolution proceedings (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=7410.)
  "(a) Except as provided in subdivision (b), no corporation shall make any distribution except upon dissolution. (b) A corporation may, subject to meeting the requirements of Sections 7412 and 7413 and any additional restrictions authorized by Section 7414, purchase or redeem memberships."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 7411(a)-(b), California Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law, the prohibition on distributions except upon dissolution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=7411.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of a distinct, statute-based restriction and its scope in that one state — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation, and whether a state restricts distributions by a mutual-benefit-type nonprofit corporation, and how, varies by state. The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code § 7410 and Cal. Corp. Code § 7411, and are treated as two independent sources, not subsections of one section. This document is informational only: it does not itself form any corporation and does not determine federal tax-exempt status, which is a separate IRS determination this document does not make.

DISSOLUTION: REMAINING ASSETS MAY BE DISTRIBUTED TO MEMBERS
California's dissolution statutes for a nonprofit mutual benefit corporation state a genuinely different rule for what happens to remaining assets than the rule that applies to a nonprofit public benefit corporation. After a mutual benefit corporation's board determines that known debts and liabilities have been paid or adequately provided for, the board distributes the remaining corporate assets under a specific statutory sequence. That sequence provides that if the articles or bylaws state how remaining assets are to be disposed of, they are disposed of that way; but if the articles and bylaws do not provide a manner of disposition, the statute itself supplies a default rule: the assets "shall be distributed among the members in accordance with their respective rights therein." This default — absent a contrary articles or bylaws provision, distribution to members is exactly what the statute itself directs — is specific to a nonprofit mutual benefit corporation; other categories of California nonprofit corporation, such as a nonprofit public benefit corporation, follow different statutory dissolution-distribution rules that this clause does not describe.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "After determining that all the known debts and liabilities of a corporation in the process of winding up have been paid or adequately provided for, the board shall distribute all the remaining corporate assets in the manner provided in Sections 8715 to 8717, inclusive."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 8713(a), California Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law, the board's duty to distribute remaining assets after paying debts (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=8713.)
  "After complying with the provisions of Section 8713 and except as otherwise provided in Sections 8715 and 8716, assets held by a corporation shall be disposed of on dissolution as follows: (a) If the articles or bylaws provide the manner of disposition, the assets shall be disposed of in that manner. (b) If the articles or bylaws do not provide the manner of disposition, the assets shall be distributed among the members in accordance with their respective rights therein."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 8717(a)-(b), California Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law, the default rule distributing remaining assets among members (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=8717.)

The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code § 8713 and Cal. Corp. Code § 8717, and are treated as two independent sources, not subsections of one section. This document is informational only: it does not itself form, dissolve, or wind up any corporation, and it does not determine federal tax-exempt status, which is a separate IRS determination this document does not make — an organization that has obtained federal tax-exempt recognition under a category with its own asset-dedication requirements may face federal constraints on member distributions that this state-law default rule, by itself, does not address.

MEMBER APPROVAL REQUIRED FOR SALE OF SUBSTANTIALLY ALL ASSETS AND FOR MERGERS
California's Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law requires member approval, not board approval alone, for certain major transactions. A mutual benefit corporation may sell, lease, convey, exchange, transfer, or otherwise dispose of all or substantially all of its assets only when the principal terms are approved by the board, and — unless the transaction is in the corporation's usual and regular course of activities — also approved by the members, whose approval may come either before or after the board's approval and either before or after the transaction itself. A comparable member-approval requirement applies to mergers: the principal terms of a merger must be approved by the members of each class of each constituent corporation, in addition to whatever other approvals the articles independently require, and that member approval may likewise be given before or after the board's approval. In both cases, the statute gives members of a mutual benefit corporation a direct statutory voice in a transaction that could fundamentally change or end the corporation, beyond whatever role the board plays.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) Subject to the provisions of Section 7142, a corporation may sell, lease, convey, exchange, transfer or otherwise dispose of all or substantially all of its assets when the principal terms are: (1) Approved by the board; and (2) Unless the transaction is in the usual and regular course of its activities, approved by the members (Section 5034), either before or after approval by the board and before or after the transaction."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 7911(a), California Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law, member approval for sale of substantially all assets (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=7911.)
  "The principal terms of the merger shall be approved by the members (Section 5034) of each class of each constituent corporation and by each other person or persons whose approval of an amendment of articles is required by the articles; and the approval by the members (Section 5034) or such other person or persons required by this section may be given before or after the approval by the board."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 8012, California Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law, member approval of merger principal terms (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=8012.)

The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code § 7911 and Cal. Corp. This document is informational only: it does not itself form any corporation, does not itself effect any sale of assets or merger, and does not determine federal tax-exempt status, which is a separate IRS determination this document does not make.

NONPROFIT MUTUAL BENEFIT CORPORATION PURPOSE AND AGENT DECLARATION
The name of the corporation is Acme Trade Alliance. Acme Trade Alliance is a nonprofit mutual benefit corporation organized under the Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law. The purpose of this corporation is to engage in any lawful act or activity, other than credit union business, for which a corporation may be organized under such law. and to promote the professional interests of its members through education and networking The initial street address of Acme Trade Alliance is 500 Market St, San Francisco, CA 94105. The name of Acme Trade Alliance's initial agent for service of process in California is Jordan Alex Lee. The agent's street address in California is 500 Market St, San Francisco, CA 94105.

MUTUAL BENEFIT INCORPORATOR SIGNATURE
Executed by the incorporator:

Incorporator: Jordan Alex Lee

Signature: ☐ _________________________ Date: _______________

expectedJSON.body: California's Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law requires member approval, not board approval alone, for certain major transactions. A mutual benefit corporation may sell, lease, convey, exchange, transfer, or otherwise dispose of all or substantially all of its assets only when the principal terms are approved by the board, and — unless the transaction is in the corporation's usual and regular course of activities — also approved by the members, whose approval may come either before or after the board's approval and either before or after the transaction itself. A comparable member-approval requirement applies to mergers: the principal terms of a merger must be approved by the members of each class of each constituent corporation, in addition to whatever other approvals the articles independently require, and that member approval may likewise be given before or after the board's approval. In both cases, the statute gives members of a mutual benefit corporation a direct statutory voice in a transaction that could fundamentally change or end the corporation, beyond whatever role the board plays.

citations.quote: (a) Subject to the provisions of Section 7142, a corporation may sell, lease, convey, exchange, transfer or otherwise dispose of all or substantially all of its assets when the principal terms are: (1) Approved by the board; and (2) Unless the transaction is in the usual and regular course of its activities, approved by the members (Section 5034), either before or after approval by the board and before or after the transaction.

citations.quote: The principal terms of the merger shall be approved by the members (Section 5034) of each class of each constituent corporation and by each other person or persons whose approval of an amendment of articles is required by the articles; and the approval by the members (Section 5034) or such other person or persons required by this section may be given before or after the approval by the board.
